analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. greenhouse gas emissions with a declining, tradeable permit system and returns proceeds to consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 136 cosponsors, including 14 Republicans, but never received a single committee vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a national cap on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, factories, and oil refiners, starting in 2012, using tradeable permits: companies would have to hold one permit for every ton they emit, and the total number of permits would shrink over time. It would have created a public database of who emits what, and a nonprofit corporation that would use permit proceeds to lower energy costs for consumers, retrain workers who lose jobs, and fund clean coal, farm, and wildlife programs. The bill was referred to three House committees, sent to subcommittees, and never acted on again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, who would receive rebates and cost relief funded by permit trading, and people exposed to climate damage (coastal residents, low-income populations, wildlife). Workers in fossil-fuel-dependent communities would get transition assistance; farmers would get paid for sequestering carbon; clean-energy and low-carbon technology firms would gain a market.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a declining national cap on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, industry, and transportation fuels, falling from 6,150 million metric tons to 1,504 million metric tons per year after 2049.
Requires the Climate Change Credit Corporation to use permit proceeds to reduce costs borne by consumers, with preferential treatment for those least able to afford higher energy prices.
Directs 20% of permit proceeds in 2012 (declining over ten years) to transition assistance for dislocated workers and their communities.
Creates a public, searchable National Greenhouse Gas Database of who emits what, with annual public reporting.
Funds farm conservation, wind energy on agricultural land, coastal adaptation planning, and wildlife habitat restoration to help fish and wildlife adjust to climate change.

analysis.who_pays: Large emitters: electric utilities, oil refiners and importers, and industrial facilities emitting over 10,000 metric tons a year, who must surrender permits per ton or pay a civil penalty worth triple the market value of the missing permits. They can pass some of this cost to consumers through higher energy prices, though the bill channels permit proceeds back to consumers to offset it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Utilities, refiners, and large industrial emitters

drawbacks.text: Large emitters receive most tradeable allowances at no cost, and early actors get extra bonus allowances, handing a valuable new asset to the industries being regulated rather than auctioning permits for public revenue.

Covered entities can meet up to 15% of their obligation with offsets and international credits, plus 20% more if they sign an accelerated-participation agreement they can terminate at any time, which could weaken real domestic emission reductions.

The Administrator may exempt source categories that are hard to measure (though not fossil-fuel carbon dioxide), and the cap's stringency would depend on regulatory determinations reviewed only biennially.
Compliance costs for utilities and refiners would likely be passed to consumers as higher energy prices until consumer relief programs ramp up.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have established the first binding national cap on U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, with real penalties, a shrinking limit, and unusually strong consumer and worker protections: proceeds flow to consumer rebates, aid for dislocated workers, and low-income households. Its main weakness is design, not intent: giving permits free to the largest emitters creates windfall assets for polluters and forgoes public revenue an auction would have raised, and the generous offset and borrowing provisions could soften the cap's bite in early years. On balance it is a genuine climate policy aimed at a public good, with costs concentrated on fossil-fuel-heavy industries and partially returned to consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees and their subcommittees from January 2007 onward; no committee ever reported it out, and it died without a vote when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. John Olver introduced the Climate Stewardship Act of 2007 in the House on January 22, 2007.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Science and Technology, and Natural Resources committees, and within two weeks was sent to subcommittees in each.
No committee or subcommittee ever held a markup or reported the bill; the only actions in its history are the referrals.
The bill attracted 136 cosponsors, including 122 Democrats and 14 Republicans, giving it more than tripartisan-ample signers for a House majority, but it never reached the floor.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and all unreported bills die with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large greenhouse-gas emitters — electric utilities, coal-fired power, oil refiners, and heavy industry — stayed better off, because no cap on their emissions ever took effect during this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large emitters avoided an emissions cap

for.name: Rep. John Olver
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 17 original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 14 of 202 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Gilchrest, Kirk, Castle, Shays, and Saxton among the original signers.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee on February 2, 2007, and never held a markup or reported the bill.

against.name: House Science and Technology and Natural Resources Committees
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees (Energy and Environment; Fisheries, Wildlife, and Oceans) and never acted further.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 122 Democrats and 14 Republicans of the 136 cosponsors — but the bill died in committee without a vote, so the parties' full memberships were never recorded on it.

industries.note: Utilities would have to surrender a permit for every ton emitted, but would receive most allowances free, get bonus allowances for early or accelerated action, and be eligible for coal gasification and carbon-capture grants (at least 20% reserved for rural electric cooperatives). Their interest in the bill ran against consumers, since compliance costs would be passed through energy prices until rebates offset them.

Refiners and importers would submit allowances for every unit of transportation fuel sold, directly pricing the emissions from gasoline and diesel they sell. The bill's stated aim of reducing dependence on foreign oil cuts against their core product.

Farmers could sell registered soil-carbon sequestration offsets to covered entities and receive grants for wind energy, conservation practices, and renewable fuels on agricultural land, funded by the Climate Change Credit Corporation.
A declining cap and allowance-funded deployment programs (geological carbon storage, cellulosic biomass, efficiency upgrades) would create demand and financing for low-carbon technology.

Emissions from burning coal would be priced under the cap, but the bill funds coal gasification plants that capture and store at least 90% of their carbon dioxide, a partial lifeline for coal in electricity generation.

Allowance proceeds fund habitat restoration, state climate mitigation plans, coastal adaptation assistance, and NOAA reporting on ocean and fishery impacts, all directed at protecting resources these industries depend on.
